body.heading: The square in the engraving
paragraphs: Albrecht Dürer's engraving Melencolia I, made in 1514, shows a winged figure surrounded by tools, an hourglass, a strange solid — and, on the wall behind her, a four-by-four magic square. Its rows, columns and diagonals all add to 34.
The square reads: 16, 3, 2, 13 across the top; then 5, 10, 11, 8; then 9, 6, 7, 12; and 4, 15, 14, 1 along the bottom. Add any full row or column and you will land on 34 every time.

body.heading: The date in the corner
paragraphs: Look at the bottom row: 4, 15, 14, 1. The two middle numbers are 15 and 14 — the year 1514, the year Dürer made the engraving. He signed his puzzle with its own birthday.

The square hides more patterns. The four corner cells (16, 13, 4 and 1) add to 34. So do the four cells in the very centre (10, 11, 6 and 7). Dürer chose an arrangement mathematicians call “most-perfect” in spirit: it keeps giving 34 wherever you probe it.

body.heading: Try it: hunt for 34
paragraphs: Copy Dürer's square onto paper and hunt for sets of four cells that make 34. Try the four corners of any smaller two-by-two block inside it — several of them work. Keep a tally of how many different sets you can find.

Then try the artist's trick yourself: build a three-by-three magic square (every line making 15) and see whether you can arrange it so the bottom row hides a number that matters to you, like a birthday.

takeaway: Dürer's square is a puzzle, a signature and a date stamp in one: art and arithmetic sharing the same sixteen cells.
